paras.A: In the middle of the twentieth century, bicycles seemed to belong to the past. As cars became cheaper, families in Europe and North America sold their bikes, and city roads were rebuilt for traffic rather than for people. By the 1970s, in many large cities, only children and a few enthusiasts still rode to school or work. Bicycle factories closed, repair shops disappeared, and a generation grew up believing that a normal adult travels by car.
paras.B: Then oil prices rose sharply, and drivers began to think again. At the same time, doctors reported that people were taking much less exercise than before. Some city governments reacted quickly. Copenhagen built separate lanes for cyclists in the 1980s, and today more than half of its residents travel to work or school by bicycle. Other cities were slower, mainly because planners worried that shops would lose customers if parking spaces disappeared.
paras.C: In fact, research suggests the opposite. When a busy street in Toronto replaced a few parking spaces with a cycle lane, the shops along it earned more money, not less. Cyclists stop more often than drivers, and they tend to visit local businesses on the way home. A car, by contrast, needs a large space for only one or two shoppers, and most drivers prefer to park outside big supermarkets.
paras.D: Cycling is not without problems. In wet or cold weather, fewer people ride, and cities with steep hills find it harder to persuade residents to leave their cars at home. Safety is another worry, since many parents will not allow children on busy roads. Electric bicycles have helped with hills and long distances, and they are particularly popular among older riders. Another difficulty is theft: in some cities, owners lose a bicycle every few years, and many people therefore keep an old, cheap one for daily use.
paras.E: Experts agree that the best way to encourage cycling is to make it feel safe. This means protected lanes with a barrier between bikes and cars, rather than a painted line on the road. Several cities now also offer bike-sharing schemes, in which visitors can borrow a bicycle for a few minutes and leave it at any station. Such schemes cost money to start, but they cost far less than building a new road.

paras.A: Tea is the most popular drink in the world after water, yet its story began as a simple accident, or so a famous legend says. According to the legend, a Chinese ruler was sitting under a tree while his servant boiled water. A few leaves from the tree blew into the pot, and the ruler liked the smell so much that he tasted the drink. Historians doubt that the story is true, but they agree that tea was first used in China more than two thousand years ago.
paras.B: At first, tea was a medicine rather than a pleasure. Monks drank it to stay awake during long hours of prayer, and doctors recommended it for headaches. Over time, wealthy families began to serve it to guests, and a special ceremony developed in Japan, where the preparation of a single cup can take half an hour. The ceremony teaches patience and respect, and it is still practised in many homes and schools today.
paras.C: Tea reached Europe in the seventeenth century on Dutch and Portuguese ships. It was so expensive that people kept it in locked boxes, and only rich households could afford a cup. In Britain, demand grew quickly, and the government raised taxes on it. Some merchants responded by bringing tea into the country secretly, so that they did not have to pay. This illegal trade became so large that, for a time, more tea was smuggled than sold legally.
paras.D: Today, tea is grown in many warm, wet regions, including India, Kenya and Sri Lanka. The leaves are picked by hand, dried and then packed. Black tea and green tea come from the same plant; the difference lies in the way the leaves are treated after picking. Green tea is dried quickly, whereas black tea is left to change colour in the air before drying. Each method gives the drink a different taste.
paras.E: Many people drink tea for comfort as well as taste. In some countries, offering a cup to a visitor is a sign of friendship, and refusing it may seem rude. Scientists are still studying whether tea is good for health. Some studies suggest small benefits, but experts advise drinking it in moderation, especially in the evening, because it contains caffeine and may make it harder to sleep.

paras.A: Every Saturday morning, a group of about thirty people meets at the gate of Riverside Park. They are not tourists or joggers. They are volunteers, and they give up their free time to clean and care for the park. The group was started by a retired teacher, who became upset when she saw rubbish lying near the pond. She put a notice on a tree, and the first week, only four people came.
paras.B: Today the work is organised carefully. Some volunteers collect rubbish with long sticks and bags, while others plant flowers or repair old benches. A small team looks after the pond and checks the water. Children are welcome, but they must stay with an adult. The volunteers wear bright yellow jackets so that visitors can easily see who to ask for help.
paras.C: Why do people give their time for free? When the group were asked, their answers were very different. Some said they wanted to meet neighbours, because they had recently moved to the area. paras.D: The council has noticed the difference. Fewer people drop rubbish in the park than before, and the number of birds has increased. paras.E: Anyone can join. No experience is necessary, and there is no fee. New volunteers usually start with an easy job, such as sweeping paths, and they can try other tasks later. title: Learning to Swim as an Adult

paras.A: Many people believe that learning to swim is something you do as a child. If you missed it, they say, it is too late. This is not true. Every year, thousands of adults begin swimming lessons, and many of them become confident swimmers within a few months. Teachers say that adults often start with a handicap, though, and that handicap is fear.
paras.B: The fear usually has a cause. Some adults had a bad experience in water when they were young, such as falling into a river or being pushed into a pool. Others simply grew up in a place where there was no water nearby. Whatever the reason, the body reacts in the same way: the heart beats faster, the muscles become stiff and breathing becomes shallow. Stiff muscles make it harder to float, so fear can make the problem worse.
paras.C: Good teachers therefore begin slowly. In the first lessons, students may stand in shallow water and only practise breathing out under the surface. They learn to float on their backs with a teacher's hand underneath, and then without it. Only when they feel safe do they move on to arm and leg movements. Some pools offer private lessons for adults, so that nobody feels embarrassed in front of children.
paras.D: Adults also have advantages. They can understand instructions better than young children, and they know why each exercise is useful. Many are motivated by a clear goal, such as joining their children on holiday or recovering from a sports injury. Doctors often recommend swimming because it exercises the whole body without hurting the joints, which is especially valuable for people who are no longer young.
paras.E: Progress varies, but most adults can swim a short distance after about ten lessons. The best advice from experienced teachers is to attend regularly and to be patient with yourself. One former student says that the moment she swam across the pool for the first time was one of the proudest of her life. She was fifty-two.

paras.A: When people think of a library, they often imagine a quiet room with rows of old books. Some libraries still look like this, but many have changed greatly in the last twenty years. Today a city library may have computers, quiet study rooms, a café, a children's theatre and even a room where visitors can borrow tools. Librarians say that the building is no longer only a place for books; it is a place for the whole community, young and old.
paras.B: One reason for the change is technology. Many people now read newspapers and novels on screens, and they may not visit a library as often as their parents did. To keep readers interested, libraries lend electronic books that can be downloaded at home. Others offer free internet for people who do not own a computer. This service is especially valuable for job-seekers, who need to send applications online.
paras.C: Libraries have also become places to learn new skills. In many towns, they organise classes in languages, computer use and cooking. Older residents attend lessons on how to use a smartphone, and teenagers come after school to do homework in a quiet space. Because the classes are free, they attract people who could not afford a private course.
paras.D: Not everyone is happy with the changes. Some readers complain that libraries have become too noisy and that there are fewer books on the shelves. Librarians reply that the number of books has not fallen; they are simply stored differently, and visitors can order any book that is not on display. They add that a library without people would not survive, whatever it contained.
paras.E: The libraries of the future will probably continue to change. A few have already introduced robots that help visitors find books, and some plan to open at night. Yet most librarians believe that the basic idea will remain the same: a library offers free access to knowledge for everybody. As long as that idea matters, they say, there will be a place for the library.

paras.A: In many countries, a large part of daily eating happens on the street. Stalls and small carts sell hot meals at low prices, and they are often crowded at lunchtime. For workers who have little time and little money, street food is the easiest way to get a good meal. It is also a great attraction for visitors, who say that they learn more about a city from one evening at a food stall than from a week of sightseeing.
paras.B: Each region has its own favourites. In Mexico, many vendors sell small tortillas filled with meat, onions and a hot sauce. In Thailand, the smell of frying noodles fills the air in the evening. In Turkey, a popular snack is bread with grilled fish, which is sold near the sea. Although the dishes are different, they share one feature: they can be prepared quickly in front of the customer.
paras.C: Street food is more than food; it is also a way of earning a living. Millions of families depend on small stalls, and the skills are often passed from parent to child. A vendor may start work at four in the morning to buy ingredients at the market and prepare them before the first customers arrive. The work is hard, and the income depends on the weather.
paras.D: Safety is a common concern. Visitors worry that food cooked outdoors may make them ill. Experts offer simple advice: choose a stall that is busy, because a high number of customers means the food is fresh, and look for food that is cooked in front of you at a high temperature. Drinking bottled water is also sensible in places where the tap water is not safe.
paras.E: Some cities are trying to control street food, claiming that stalls cause traffic jams and rubbish. Others encourage it by creating special markets where vendors receive training and clean water. The second approach seems to be more successful. It keeps the tradition alive while improving hygiene, and it gives customers confidence. After all, the best street food depends on trust between the cook and the person who eats.

paras.A: For hundreds of years, people have used the wind. Sailors crossed the oceans in ships with large sails, and farmers built windmills to grind grain and pump water. The earliest windmills appeared in Persia more than a thousand years ago, and later versions spread through Europe. In the twentieth century, engineers discovered that the same principle could be used to make electricity.
paras.B: A modern wind turbine looks like a giant three-bladed propeller on a tall tower. When the wind turns the blades, they rotate a shaft that drives a generator inside. The bigger the blades and the higher the tower, the more power is produced, because wind is stronger and steadier at height. The largest turbines are taller than a thirty-storey building, and a single machine can supply electricity to thousands of homes.
paras.C: Wind power has many advantages. Once a turbine is built, the wind costs nothing, and the electricity produced does not release the gases that warm the planet. Wind farms can be placed in open fields, where farmers continue to grow crops between the towers, or at sea, where the wind is stronger. Several countries now produce a large part of their electricity in this way, and the price of wind energy has fallen sharply over the last twenty years.
paras.D: However, wind power is not perfect. The wind does not blow all the time, so the electricity supply goes up and down. For this reason, countries must keep other power stations or large batteries ready for calm days. Some people dislike the appearance of turbines in beautiful landscapes, and others complain about the noise. Birds and bats are sometimes killed by the blades, and engineers are looking for ways to reduce this problem, for example by stopping turbines during migration.
paras.E: Uzbekistan has large areas of open, sunny and windy land, and the government is building wind and solar farms in the desert regions. Experts believe that in the future, the country could export clean electricity to its neighbours. Whether wind will become the main source of power remains uncertain, but it is clear that the old windmills have found a new life, and that the breeze can help to run the modern world.

paras.A: Thirty years ago, very few children owned a mobile phone. Today, in many countries, most children have one by the age of twelve, and some receive their first phone at seven or eight. Parents give them for good reasons: a phone helps to stay in touch, to call for help in an emergency and to find directions. At the same time, many adults worry about the amount of time young people spend on their screens.
paras.B: Researchers have found both benefits and risks. On the positive side, phones give access to a huge amount of information. A student can look up a word, watch a video about a science experiment or join an online class. Phones also allow friends who live far apart to share photographs and messages, which can be a great comfort to a child who has moved to a new school.
paras.C: On the negative side, too much screen time may affect sleep and concentration. Children who use phones late at night often feel tired the next day, and those who check messages every few minutes find it hard to focus on homework. Some young people compare themselves with the perfect pictures they see online and begin to feel unhappy about their own lives. There is also the danger of meeting strangers or of seeing material that is not suitable for their age.
paras.D: Experts advise parents not to forbid phones completely, but to set clear rules. A common recommendation is to keep phones out of the bedroom at night, and to agree on periods without screens, such as meals and family evenings. Parents can also install programmes that block unsuitable websites. Most important, they should talk to their children about what they do online and encourage them to say if something makes them uncomfortable.
paras.E: Children also learn by watching adults. A mother who looks at her phone throughout dinner cannot easily ask her son to put his away. If the whole family reduces its screen time and finds enjoyable alternatives, such as walks, board games or cooking together, the rules become easier to follow. As one psychologist puts it, 'We cannot ask children to be better with technology than we are.'

paras.A: The word photography comes from two Greek words meaning 'drawing with light'. The idea is not new. More than a thousand years ago, scholars noticed that when light passes through a tiny hole into a dark room, it produces an upside-down image of the outside scene on the opposite wall. This simple effect was used by artists, who traced the image to help them draw. However, nobody knew how to keep the picture permanently.
paras.B: The breakthrough came in the 1820s, when a French inventor named Nicéphore Niépce succeeded in recording an image on a metal plate covered with a light-sensitive material. The exposure took many hours, and the result was blurred. A few years later, another Frenchman, Louis Daguerre, improved the process so that a picture could be made in a few minutes. His 'daguerreotypes' were sharp and detailed, and the news soon spread around the world.
paras.C: Photography changed society quickly. Before the camera, only the rich could afford a painted portrait. Now, families could have a picture of themselves for a small price. Photographers travelled to distant countries and brought back pictures of places that people had only read about. During wars, photographs showed what really happened, and they sometimes changed public opinion more strongly than a thousand words.
paras.D: The next big step came in 1888, when George Eastman introduced a simple box camera with a roll of film under the slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest'. Suddenly, anyone could take photographs. Colour film followed in the 1930s, and in the 1970s, scientists built the first digital camera. Today, nearly every phone has a camera, and people take billions of pictures every day.
paras.E: With so many images, one might think photography has lost its value. Yet many experts believe the opposite. They say that the pleasure of choosing a moment, composing a picture and looking at the result is as strong as ever. A good photographer, they say, does not just record what is there, but shows how it feels to be there. And that, in the end, is why some pictures are remembered for a hundred years.

paras.A: Earthquakes can happen without warning. The ground begins to shake, objects fall from shelves and buildings may crack or collapse. Most injuries are not caused by the shaking itself but by falling objects and broken glass. The good news is that people who know what to do can greatly reduce their risk. Experts say that the best protection is preparation.
paras.B: Before an earthquake, there are several simple steps. Heavy furniture, such as bookshelves and wardrobes, should be fixed to the wall so that it cannot fall on people. Heavy objects should be kept on the lower shelves. Every family should have an emergency kit in a place that is easy to reach. It should contain water, food that does not spoil, a torch, a radio with spare batteries and a first-aid box.
paras.C: When the shaking starts, the advice is to 'drop, cover and hold on'. Drop to your hands and knees, so that you cannot be knocked over. Cover your head and neck with your arms, and, if possible, go under a strong table. Hold on until the shaking stops. Running outside is dangerous, because bricks and glass may fall from buildings. If you are outdoors, move away from buildings, trees and electric wires to an open space.
paras.D: After the main shock, smaller tremors called aftershocks may follow, sometimes for days. People should be ready to drop, cover and hold on again. Before leaving a building, check for gas leaks: if you smell gas, open a window and go outside at once, and do not use matches or switches. Use the telephone only for emergencies, so that the lines remain free for rescue workers.
paras.E: Schools in earthquake regions often hold regular practice drills so that children know exactly what to do. In Tashkent, many schools and apartment blocks have special exits and meeting places. Teachers say that calm and clear instructions are the key. Children who have practised the steps usually react quickly and without panic, and this can make the difference between safety and danger.

paras.A: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of routes that connected China with the Mediterranean. It got its name from the most valuable product carried along it, silk, which the Chinese kept secret for centuries. However, merchants traded many other goods: spices, glass, horses, gold, paper and precious stones. A trader who completed the whole journey would have been away from home for years, so most merchants travelled only part of the way.
paras.B: The journey was difficult. Caravans of camels crossed deserts where temperatures were extremely high and water was scarce, and mountain passes where snow could close the route for weeks. Thieves attacked the weak, and storms buried the tracks. To reduce the risk, traders travelled in large groups and paid guides who knew the paths. They stopped at caravanserais, fortified inns in which they could rest, trade and keep their animals safe.
paras.C: Cities in present-day Uzbekistan, such as Samarkand and Bukhara, became rich because they stood at the centre of the network. Merchants from China, India, Persia and Europe met in their bazaars, exchanged goods and shared news. The cities were also places for exchanging ideas. Scientists, poets and craftsmen of different cultures learned from each other, and new techniques such as papermaking travelled in the same caravans as the goods.
paras.D: Not only products travelled along the Silk Road, but also religions, languages and illnesses. Buddhism spread from India to China, Islam grew across Central Asia, and the plague, tragically, moved with the traders and reached Europe in the fourteenth century. The mix of cultures left traces that can still be seen in the food, music and architecture of the region.
paras.E: The old routes declined when ships began to carry goods directly by sea, which was cheaper and faster. Yet the memory of the Silk Road remains strong, and in recent years, governments have built new railways and highways along the old paths. In 2014, parts of the route were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list. For many travellers, a journey to Samarkand or Bukhara is a chance to follow in the steps of the ancient merchants.

title: Giving Old Clothes a New Life

paras.A: Every year, the world produces more than a hundred billion items of clothing. Many of them are cheap, and shoppers can afford to replace them often. A shirt that is worn five times and then thrown away is not unusual. The result is a mountain of textile waste: in some countries, each person throws away more than thirty kilograms of clothes annually, and most of it ends up in rubbish dumps.
paras.B: The environmental cost is high. Producing a single cotton shirt takes thousands of litres of water, and factories that dye cloth often release coloured chemicals into rivers. When synthetic clothes are washed, they release tiny pieces of plastic that finally reach the sea. Experts therefore say that the most environmentally friendly garment is the one that already exists in your wardrobe.
paras.C: An old idea is returning: repair. A torn seam or a lost button can be fixed in minutes, and many towns now have repair cafés, where volunteers help people mend their clothes for free. Learning basic sewing is simple, and it gives satisfaction as well as saving money. Some schools have even restarted lessons in needlework, and children discover that making a bag from an old pair of jeans is great fun.
paras.D: Another solution is to pass clothes on. Second-hand shops, school swaps and online markets allow clothes to find new owners. Children, who grow quickly, benefit especially, since a coat that is too small for one child will fit another. In some neighbourhoods, families organise 'swap parties', where everyone brings clothes they no longer need and takes home something new to them.
paras.E: Finally, recycling is developing. Companies have started to turn old cotton into new thread, and some even make fibre from used plastic bottles. The technology is still expensive, and not every material can be recycled, but progress is encouraging. Shoppers can help by asking a simple question before every purchase: 'Will I wear this at least thirty times?' If the answer is no, perhaps it is better not to buy it.

paras.A: A bee colony works like a small town. In a single hive, there may be forty thousand bees, and every one of them has a job. One bee, the queen, lays eggs. The other bees, nearly all female, are called workers, and they do everything else. Their jobs change as they grow older, and a worker bee may be a nurse, a builder, a guard and a food collector during her short life.
paras.B: Young workers stay inside the hive. First they clean the cells where eggs are laid, and then they feed the young bees. Later they build new cells from wax, which comes from special glands in their bodies. At about three weeks old, a worker becomes a guard and stands at the entrance to the hive. Her task is to stop other insects from coming in, and she can recognise a stranger by its smell.
paras.C: Only the oldest workers leave the hive to find food. They fly several kilometres to visit flowers, collecting a sweet liquid called nectar and a yellow powder called pollen. Back at the hive, a bee that has found a good field of flowers tells the others about it by dancing. The direction of the dance shows where the flowers are, and the speed shows how far away they are.
paras.D: The nectar is turned into honey inside the hive. Bees put it in wax cells and fan it with their wings until most of the water has gone. Then they close the cell with a thin layer of wax. This honey is food for the colony in winter, when there are no flowers. A beekeeper usually takes only the extra honey and leaves enough for the bees.
paras.E: Bees are important for people, too. While they visit flowers, they carry pollen from one plant to another, and this allows many fruits and vegetables to grow. Without bees, apples, almonds and many other foods would be much harder to produce. Because of this, farmers in several countries now protect wild flowers near their fields, in order to give bees a place to live and feed.

paras.A: For many centuries, people wrote on materials that were difficult to make or hard to carry. In China, long before our era, writers used thin strips of bamboo or pieces of silk. paras.A: Moving to a new city is exciting, but it is rarely easy. In the first week, everything feels different: the streets, the shops, even the sound of the traffic. A person who has left family and friends behind may feel lonely, however busy the new city seems. paras.B: Practical problems come first. A newcomer must find a place to live, open a bank account, register with a doctor and learn how the public transport works. Each of these tasks takes time, and mistakes are common. One man from a small town admitted that he spent his first month taking the wrong bus every morning. Experts advise making a list and doing one task at a time, rather than trying to solve everything in a day.
paras.C: Making friends is harder than it sounds. Adults do not have the daily routine of a school or a university, where it is natural to meet people. Instead, they must create opportunities. paras.D: Some people try to keep their old life intact by calling their friends every day and visiting home every weekend. This is understandable, but it can slow down the process of settling in. paras.E: Many people say that a move teaches them something about themselves. They become more independent, learn to ask for help and discover interests they did not know they had. paras.A: Sending a message used to be a slow and uncertain business. In ancient times, rulers used fast riders to carry letters across their empires, but ordinary people had no such service. A citizen who wanted to send news to a relative in another town had to find a traveller who was going the same way and ask a favour. The letter might arrive in a month, or it might never arrive at all.
paras.B: The modern postal system began in the nineteenth century, when Britain introduced the first stamp. Before that, the person who received a letter usually paid for it, and many people refused to take letters that cost too much. The new system was simple: the sender bought a small piece of paper, stuck it on the envelope, and the post office delivered the letter anywhere in the country for the same price. The number of letters increased enormously.
paras.C: For a hundred years, trains made the service faster. Mail was sorted on board while the train was moving, so that letters were ready for delivery at the next station. Aeroplanes, and later computers, brought new changes. Today a letter can cross a continent in a few days, and in many countries, post offices also offer banking, passport services and parcel delivery.
paras.D: Email, of course, has reduced the number of personal letters. Few people now write to friends on paper, and postmen carry more advertisements and bills than letters. On the other hand, online shopping has created an enormous growth in parcels. Postal workers say that their work has become heavier, and that they now spend more time lifting boxes than delivering envelopes.
paras.E: Yet the handwritten letter has not disappeared. Many people keep letters from grandparents or friends for years, and receiving one still feels special. A message on a phone can be deleted in a second, but a letter is an object that can be touched and kept. For this reason, some people predict that, even in the future, the postal service will continue to deliver at least a few thousand cards and letters every week.

title: Navruz: A New Year in Spring

paras.A: In Uzbekistan and many neighbouring countries, the new year does not begin in winter. It begins on the day of the spring equinox, around the twenty-first of March, when day and night are of equal length. This festival is called Navruz, which means 'new day'. It is more than two thousand years old, and for many families it is the most important celebration of the year.
paras.B: Preparations start weeks in advance. Houses are cleaned from top to bottom, old things are thrown away, and families buy new clothes for the children. People also try to pay their debts and forget old quarrels, because it is believed that the year will go well if it begins in peace. Schools hold concerts and competitions, and in many towns, workers plant trees along the streets.
paras.C: Food is at the centre of the festival. The most famous dish is sumalak, a sweet, thick paste made from sprouted wheat. It is cooked in a large pot for many hours, sometimes through the whole night, and the women who stir it sing songs while they wait. Everybody who passes by is welcome to taste it. Many people say that the long preparation and the shared work are as important as the dish itself.
paras.D: On the day itself, the streets and squares are full of life. Musicians play, wrestlers compete on carpets spread on the grass, and children watch the performances of traditional horse games. People visit relatives and neighbours, bringing small gifts and sweets. A saying tells that whoever is kind and generous on the first day of Navruz will be lucky for the whole year.
paras.E: Navruz is celebrated by hundreds of millions of people in different countries, and in 2010 the United Nations recognised it as an international holiday. Although customs vary from place to place, they share the same message: nature is waking up, and people should wake up with it. The festival connects the past with the future, and it invites everybody, young and old, to begin again.

paras.A: Fifty years ago, the Aral Sea in Central Asia was one of the largest lakes in the world. Fishing boats sailed on its blue water, and the towns on its shore lived from fish and tourism. In the town of Moynaq, a large factory prepared tinned fish that was sold across the country. Today the same town is hundreds of kilometres from the water, and old ships lie in the sand.
paras.B: The sea began to shrink in the 1960s. The two rivers that supplied it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, were used to water the fields of cotton and rice across the desert. Canals were built to carry the water, and many of them lost much of it by leaking into the ground. Less and less water reached the sea, and its surface became smaller each year.
paras.C: The consequences were severe. As the water level dropped, the salt in the water became stronger, and the fish could not survive. Thousands of fishermen lost their jobs, and many families left. The dry bed of the sea turned into a desert, where wind carried dust and salt into nearby villages. People complained of health problems, and the local climate became hotter in summer and colder in winter.
paras.D: In recent years, some efforts have been made to help. A dam was built across part of the northern Aral Sea in Kazakhstan, and the water level in that section has risen. Fish have returned, and fishermen have begun to work again. In Uzbekistan, scientists and local people have planted a forest of salt-tolerant trees on the dry sea bed, which helps to stop the dust.
paras.E: The story of the Aral Sea is often used as a warning. It shows how large projects can damage nature when planners ignore the long-term effects. At the same time, it also shows that recovery is possible when governments, scientists and local communities work together. The sea will probably never return to its former size, but small steps can still bring life back to some parts of the region.

paras.B: The preparation is a skill, and it is traditionally the work of men. A cook, called an oshpaz, begins by heating oil in a large, round pot called a kazan. He fries the onions until they are golden, adds the meat and then the carrots, which are cut into long thin strips. Water and spices are added, and the mixture simmers slowly to make a rich sauce known as zirvak. Only then is the rice placed on top.
paras.C: The timing is important. If the rice is cooked too long, it becomes sticky; if it is cooked too briefly, it remains hard. The cook watches the pot carefully, makes holes in the rice with a wooden stick to let the steam escape and covers it with a lid. paras.D: There are many regional variations. In Samarkand, the rice is often cooked with chickpeas and raisins, and the plov is eaten in the morning. paras.E: Plov also has a social meaning. In a neighbourhood, groups of men often take turns to host a plov evening, and the custom strengthens friendship. In 2016, the dish was added to a list of cultural traditions protected by an international organisation. For many people, the taste of plov means home, and for visitors, it is one of the best ways of getting to know the country.

paras.A: The Fergana Valley, in the east of Uzbekistan, has been a centre of silk production for many centuries. Mulberry trees grow along every irrigation canal, and in spring families put silkworms on trays of fresh leaves. In less than a month, the worms grow to a thousand times their original weight and then wrap themselves in cocoons of fine thread. A single cocoon can contain a thread longer than one kilometre.
paras.B: To make silk, workers place the cocoons in hot water. The heat loosens the thread, which is then wound onto a wheel. Several threads are twisted together to make a stronger one. In traditional workshops this work is done by hand, and a skilled worker can prepare only a few hundred grams in a day. The result is a soft and shiny fibre that has been prized for its beauty since ancient times.
paras.C: The valley is best known for a method of decorating cloth called ikat, which local people call abr, meaning 'cloud'. Before weaving, the threads are tied and dipped into dye in several stages. Each stage adds a new colour to the pattern. The weaver must remember how the threads will meet, because even a small mistake spoils the design. The finished cloth has soft edges, as if the colours were painted on water.
paras.D: In the past, ikat was a sign of wealth, and ordinary people wore plain cotton. In the twentieth century, factory production changed the craft, and many workshops closed. Since the 1990s, however, there has been a revival. In the town of Margilan, a large workshop now employs hundreds of weavers, and visitors can watch every step, from the cocoon to the finished robe.
paras.E: Designers around the world have noticed the beauty of this cloth. Dresses and scarves made from ikat appear in fashion shows in Paris and New York, and some young designers from Uzbekistan combine traditional patterns with modern shapes. Weavers say that they are happy to see their work admired abroad, but that the most important thing is to keep the skills alive and to teach the next generation.

paras.A: Chocolate begins its life on a tree. The cacao tree grows only in hot, wet regions near the equator, and its large fruits, called pods, grow directly from the trunk. Inside each pod, there are about forty beans surrounded by a white, sweet pulp. Farmers cut the pods open with a knife, take out the beans and leave them in the sun. At this point, the beans taste bitter and nobody would want to eat them.
paras.B: The magic happens during the next steps. First, the beans are placed in boxes and covered with leaves for about a week. The heat inside the boxes makes them ferment, and this gives chocolate its typical smell. Then the beans are spread out to dry. Once they are dry, they are packed in sacks and sent by ship to factories, often in countries thousands of kilometres from where they grew.
paras.C: In the factory, the beans are roasted and the shells are removed. The inner part is ground into a thick brown liquid. Milk chocolate has more sugar and also milk powder, which makes it lighter in colour and softer in taste.
paras.D: The first people to drink chocolate were the Maya and the Aztecs in Central America. They mixed ground beans with water and spices, and the drink was bitter, not sweet. Only in the nineteenth century did inventors find a way to make solid chocolate, which could be sold cheaply in bars.
paras.E: Today, chocolate is a global business, but many cacao farmers earn very little. Some live in small villages, and their children help in the fields instead of going to school. Several companies now promise to pay fairer prices and to check how the beans are produced. Shoppers can look for a special label on the packet. By choosing carefully, they can enjoy their chocolate and help the people who grow it.

paras.A: If you use a computer or a smartphone, you use algorithms every day. An algorithm is a set of clear steps for solving a problem, and the word itself comes from the name of a scholar who lived about twelve hundred years ago. His name was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, and he was born in Khwarazm, in what is now Uzbekistan. When his name was translated into Latin, it became 'Algoritmi', and later 'algorithm'.
paras.B: Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad, in a famous centre of learning called the House of Wisdom. There, scholars from different countries translated books, discussed ideas and carried out experiments. The ruler paid them well because he believed that knowledge was valuable for the whole state. Al-Khwarizmi became one of the most respected members of the group and wrote works on mathematics, geography and astronomy.
paras.C: His most famous book is about solving equations. It describes how to find an unknown number by moving parts of an equation from one side to the other. The Arabic title of the book contained the word 'al-jabr', meaning 'restoring' or 'completing'. This word later became 'algebra'. The book used clear examples from everyday life, such as dividing land between heirs, so that readers without special training could follow the method.
paras.D: Another of his works introduced the decimal system, with the numbers from zero to nine, to the Islamic world and later to Europe. Before this, many people calculated with Roman numerals, which made long sums extremely difficult. The new system, in which the place of a digit shows its value, made calculation much faster. Today we use it so naturally that we forget someone had to explain it.
paras.E: Al-Khwarizmi also drew maps and prepared tables of the positions of the stars. In many ways, his work shows how scientific ideas travel: they begin in one place, are improved in another, and eventually become part of everyday life everywhere. In Uzbekistan, his name is honoured in schools and universities, and a statue of him stands in his home region. Each time we search the internet, we are, in a sense, using an idea that started with him.

paras.A: Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Instead, they have strong flippers that work like short wings under the water, and with them they can swim faster than most people can run. Most of the eighteen species live in the southern half of the world. Contrary to popular belief, not all of them live in ice and snow: some species are found on warm coasts of Africa and South America.
paras.B: The emperor penguin is the largest species, and it lives in the coldest place on Earth, Antarctica. They take turns moving from the cold outside to the warm centre, so that no individual stays too long at the edge.
paras.C: Their way of raising chicks is remarkable. After the female lays a single egg, she goes to the sea to feed, which may take two months. The male stays behind. When the female returns with food in her stomach, she feeds the new chick, and the father at last goes to the sea.
paras.D: Penguins have several enemies. In the water, leopard seals and orcas hunt them, and on land, large birds sometimes steal eggs. But the greatest danger today is the changing climate. paras.E: Scientists count penguins using satellite pictures, because the dark birds' droppings stain the ice and are easy to see from space. In some places, researchers also attach small devices to the birds to follow where they swim. The information helps governments to decide which parts of the ocean should be protected from fishing. Thanks to such efforts, there is hope that these remarkable birds will survive.

paras.A: A tropical rainforest is one of the busiest places on Earth. Although these forests cover less than a tenth of the land, they contain more than half of all the plant and animal species in the world. In a single hectare, scientists have counted hundreds of kinds of trees, and every tree supports its own small community of insects, birds and mosses. The air is hot and damp, and it rains almost every day.
paras.B: The forest is divided into layers. At the top are the tallest trees, which rise up to fifty metres and form a roof called the canopy. Most animals live here, because the canopy receives plenty of sunlight and fruit. Below it lies the understorey, a darker area with smaller plants. At ground level, it is so dim that only about two per cent of the sunlight arrives, and the soil is covered with fallen leaves.
paras.C: Many of the rainforest's inhabitants have strange ways of surviving. Some frogs are bright red or yellow, a warning to hunters that their skin is poisonous. Certain trees grow high roots above the ground to stay upright in the thin soil. A few plants live on the branches of other trees and collect water in their leaves, forming tiny ponds in which insects lay their eggs.
paras.D: Rainforests are important for people, even for those who never visit one. The trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen, which helps to control the climate. Many medicines come from forest plants, and scientists believe that thousands of useful substances are still waiting to be discovered. Local communities also depend on the forest for food, building materials and clean water.
paras.E: Unfortunately, rainforests are shrinking. Farmers clear land to grow crops or to keep cattle, and companies cut down trees for wood. Once the forest is gone, the thin soil quickly loses its richness, and the land can support farming for only a few years. Governments and charities are therefore working to protect the remaining forests and to plant new trees. Their message is simple: it is much easier to save a rainforest than to rebuild one.

paras.A: When it is midday in Tashkent, it is early morning in London and night in Tokyo. paras.A: Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and China, is the highest mountain on Earth. paras.B: The breakthrough came in 1953. A British expedition of several hundred people, including porters and guides, prepared for months. paras.D: The news reached London on the day of a royal ceremony, and newspapers around the world reported it. paras.E: Since then, thousands of people have climbed Everest, and the mountain has become busy. Guides now fix ropes and ladders over difficult places, and in good weather, there are queues near the top. paras.A: People have always wanted to measure time. The earliest tool was probably the sundial, in which the shadow of a stick moves around a flat surface as the sun crosses the sky. It worked well in sunny places, but it was useless at night or on cloudy days. In response, ancient peoples invented other devices, such as water clocks, in which water dripped slowly from one container into another and the level showed the passing hours.
paras.B: The first mechanical clocks appeared in Europe around the thirteenth century. They were huge, placed on towers in town centres, and they struck a bell every hour so that the townspeople could hear it. They had no face or hands at first. Their accuracy was poor, and they could lose or gain many minutes a day, so someone had to correct them regularly by looking at the sun.
paras.C: A great improvement came in the seventeenth century, when scientists discovered that a swinging weight, called a pendulum, takes the same time for each swing. A clock regulated by a pendulum lost only a few seconds a day. Soon, smaller clocks were made for houses, and later for pockets. In the eighteenth century, an English craftsman built a clock for sailors that could keep exact time during long sea voyages, which helped captains find their position.
paras.D: The twentieth century brought electric and quartz clocks, which use the regular vibrations of a small crystal. Wristwatches became cheap, and by the middle of the century, nearly everyone could own one. The most accurate clocks today are atomic clocks, which measure vibrations in atoms. Some of them lose less than one second in millions of years, and they are used in satellites, which allow phones to show our location.
paras.E: Now we live in an age when time is displayed on every screen, and yet many people feel they have too little of it. Psychologists suggest that the more precisely we measure time, the more we feel pressed by it. It may be useful, from time to time, to take off the watch, put the phone away and enjoy an hour without counting. In the end, the best clock may be the one we notice least.

paras.A: Bread is one of the oldest foods in the world, and almost every culture has its own version. The first breads were probably flat cakes made from crushed grain and water, baked on hot stones. Archaeologists have found traces of such bread more than fourteen thousand years old, long before people began to farm. Over time, bakers learned that adding a little fermented dough made the bread rise and gave it a lighter texture.
paras.B: Different countries bake different breads. In France, the long, thin loaf called the baguette is so popular that the government protects its traditional recipe. In India, thin round breads called chapatis are cooked on a flat pan and eaten with almost every meal. In Mexico, flat tortillas made from maize are used to wrap meat and vegetables. And in Central Asia, round loaves called non are baked in clay ovens, and each region has its own pattern on the top.
paras.C: In Uzbekistan, bread has a special place in the family. People believe that bread must be treated with respect. It is never placed upside down, and a piece that falls on the floor is picked up and kissed before being put aside. When guests arrive, the host often breaks a loaf and shares it, and in some regions, newly married couples taste bread at their wedding as a wish for a life without hunger.
paras.D: Making bread is a skill that takes years to learn. In a traditional bakery, the baker mixes flour, water, salt and yeast, then leaves the dough to rest for several hours. He shapes it by hand, presses the pattern into it and sticks it to the wall of the oven. The heat is fierce, and he must take each loaf out at exactly the right moment, otherwise it burns on the outside and stays soft inside.
paras.E: Modern factories now produce most of the world's bread, and supermarkets sell it sliced and packed. Many people, however, are returning to the older ways, because they prefer the taste and the smell of bread baked slowly with natural ingredients. Small bakeries are opening again, and young people are learning the craft. Perhaps this is not surprising. A fresh loaf, still warm from the oven, is one of the simplest and greatest pleasures in life.

paras.A: A kite is a simple toy, but its history is long and surprising. Historians believe that the first kites were made in China more than two thousand years ago from silk and bamboo. Early kites were not toys. Generals used them to send signals across battlefields, and fishermen used them to carry bait out over the water. Only later did the kite become a form of entertainment.
paras.B: From China, kites spread to Japan, Korea and India, and then to the Middle East and Europe. Each region developed its own style. Japanese kites are often rectangular and decorated with pictures of warriors; Indian kites are small, colourful and used in fighting competitions, in which the strings are covered with fine glass powder and the aim is to cut the opponent's kite. In Malaysia and Indonesia, enormous kites shaped like birds and moons are flown during harvest festivals.
paras.C: The science behind a kite is simple. When the wind blows against the flat surface at an angle, it pushes the kite upwards, in the same way that air lifts the wings of an aeroplane. The string keeps the kite in place, and the tail gives balance. A beginner usually learns that the best conditions are a steady breeze and plenty of open space. Trees, wires and crowds are the enemy.
paras.D: Kites have also played a role in science. In the eighteenth century, the American Benjamin Franklin flew a kite in a storm to show that lightning is electricity. A century later, meteorologists lifted instruments on kites to measure the temperature and wind high above the ground, and the Wright brothers used kites to test their ideas before building the first aeroplane.
paras.E: Today, kite flying is a popular hobby for all ages. There are annual festivals in many countries, where thousands of people gather to watch giant kites dance in the sky. Modern materials, such as nylon and carbon, make kites lighter and stronger, and some people even use them to pull boats or surfboards. Whatever the technology, the joy of watching a kite rise into the wind remains exactly the same.

paras.A: The giant panda is one of the most recognisable animals in the world. With its round black-and-white face, it appears on toys, stamps and the logos of environmental organisations. Yet in the wild, pandas are shy, solitary animals that live in cool mountain forests in central China. Fewer than two thousand of them remain, and for decades, scientists feared that the species would disappear.
paras.B: Although pandas belong to the group of animals that eat meat, almost all of their diet consists of bamboo. An adult panda eats between twelve and thirty-eight kilograms of bamboo a day and spends up to fourteen hours eating. Because bamboo gives little energy, pandas move slowly and rest for much of the day. They have a special bone in the wrist that works like a thumb, helping them to hold the stems.
paras.C: Raising young is difficult. A female usually gives birth to one or two cubs, but in the wild, often only one survives. At birth, a cub is tiny, pink and blind, and weighs about a hundred grams, which is less than a bar of chocolate. The mother takes care of it for about eighteen months, and during this time she rarely leaves it. The cub learns to climb trees early, which helps it escape from danger.
paras.D: The biggest threat to pandas has been the loss of their habitat. As farms and roads spread into the mountains, forests were cut into small pieces, and pandas could no longer find mates or enough bamboo. In response, the Chinese government created nature reserves and built green corridors that connect the separate forests. Breeding centres also help: scientists carefully study the animals and prepare some for life in the wild.
paras.E: The results have been encouraging. In 2016, the panda was moved from the list of 'endangered' to the list of 'vulnerable' species, meaning that the danger is smaller, but still real. Conservationists emphasise that the effort is not only for the panda. By protecting its forest, people also protect many other animals and plants that live there. The panda, in this sense, is a flag for a whole ecosystem.

paras.A: The city of Bukhara, in south-western Uzbekistan, is more than two thousand years old. For centuries, it was one of the main centres of trade and religion in Central Asia, and the old town contains more than a hundred protected monuments. A visitor who walks through its narrow streets feels as though he has stepped back in time, and in 1993, the historic centre was placed on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
paras.B: One of the best-known buildings is the Kalyan Minaret, a brick tower forty-five metres high. Built in the twelfth century, it was used to call people to prayer and, according to a story, as a lighthouse for caravans in the desert. When the Mongol conqueror Genghis Khan destroyed much of the city in 1220, he is said to have been so impressed by the tower that he ordered it to be left standing.
paras.C: Another feature of Bukhara is its trading domes. Several covered markets were built where main streets crossed, and each specialised in a different product: hats, jewellery, money-changing and cloth. Today, craftsmen still sell carpets, embroidery and metal work in the same halls, and the cool air under the high ceilings is welcome in the summer heat.
paras.D: Water also shaped the city. Because there was no river inside the walls, rulers built a series of ponds, called hauz, where residents could collect drinking water. The Lyabi-Hauz, the best known of them, is surrounded by old mulberry trees, two madrasahs and a caravanserai. Today, it is the centre of social life. In the evenings, families sit at tea houses, and children play near the water.
paras.E: Visitors to Bukhara often say that the real pleasure of the city is not in a single building but in the atmosphere. In the early morning, when the streets are almost empty, the sun lights up the brown bricks and turns them golden. Local people greet strangers with friendly words, and the smell of fresh bread drifts from small bakeries. For many travellers, a few days are not enough, and they promise themselves to return.

paras.A: Many people say that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. The word itself means 'breaking the fast', that is, ending the long period without food during the night. After eight or nine hours of sleep, the body needs energy, and a good breakfast helps both the body and the brain to work well. Yet in many countries, a large number of people skip it.
paras.B: Research suggests that children benefit most. Studies in several countries have found that pupils who eat breakfast concentrate better in the first lessons, remember more and behave better than those who arrive hungry. For this reason, some schools offer free meals before classes. Adults who eat breakfast also seem to eat less during the rest of the day, which can help them to keep a healthy weight, although scientists admit that the evidence is not completely clear.
paras.C: What should a good breakfast contain? Nutrition experts recommend a combination of three kinds of food. First, foods with slow energy, such as wholegrain bread or oats, provide fuel for several hours. Second, protein, which is found in eggs, cheese, yoghurt and nuts, makes the stomach feel full. Third, fruit or vegetables add vitamins. A glass of milk or a cup of tea completes a balanced meal.
paras.D: Some popular breakfasts are less healthy than they appear. Sweet cereals, pastries and many fruit drinks contain large amounts of sugar, which gives quick energy but is followed by tiredness an hour later. The best advice is to read the label on the packet and to choose products with less sugar. A simple home breakfast, such as porridge with fruit or an omelette with bread, is often better than anything from a box.
paras.E: Breakfast habits differ around the world. In Japan, many people eat rice, fish and soup. In Britain, the traditional meal includes eggs, bacon and beans. In Uzbekistan, a typical morning table has bread, butter, cream, jam, eggs and green tea. Whatever the tradition, one rule applies everywhere: sit down, take your time and enjoy it. A rushed breakfast on the street gives less benefit than a calm one at the table.

title: White Gold: The Story of Cotton

paras.A: Cotton is a plant that has clothed people for thousands of years. Its fruit, called a boll, opens when it is ripe and shows a soft white fibre that is spun into thread. In the past, cotton was so valuable that it was sometimes called 'white gold'. Today, it is grown in more than seventy countries, and Uzbekistan is one of the largest producers in the world.
paras.B: Growing cotton requires a warm climate and plenty of water. Farmers plant the seeds in spring, and the plants flower in the summer heat. After the flowers fall, the bolls develop and open in early autumn. For a long time, the harvest was done by hand, and whole families, including students and teachers, went to the fields to help. In recent decades, machines have replaced much of this manual labour.
paras.C: After picking, the cotton goes to a factory, where machines separate the fibre from the seeds. The fibre is cleaned, combed and spun into thread. Weavers then make it into cloth, which is cut and sewn into shirts, sheets, jeans and towels. Even the seeds are not wasted: they are pressed to produce cooking oil, and the remaining material is used to feed animals.
paras.D: The cotton industry has also had serious effects on the environment. The plant needs a great deal of water, and in the twentieth century, large amounts were taken from rivers to irrigate the fields in Central Asia. This was one of the main reasons why the Aral Sea began to shrink. Today, farmers use drip irrigation and other modern methods to save water, and the country has tried to grow a wider range of crops.
paras.E: Many countries now try to process cotton at home, instead of exporting the raw fibre. By making thread, cloth and clothes in local factories, they create jobs and earn more money. In Uzbekistan, new textile centres have opened, and international brands buy fabric made in the country. Nevertheless, the story of cotton is a reminder that every product has a cost, and that wise use of resources is important for future generations.

paras.A: Every year, billions of birds make long journeys across the world. This movement is called migration. In autumn, birds in the northern half of the world fly south to warmer places where food is easier to find, and in spring, they return to nest. Some of these journeys are short, but others cover many thousands of kilometres.
paras.B: Some of the greatest travellers are small birds. The Arctic tern, a light grey-and-white seabird, flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back again each year. Scientists estimate that during its life, one bird may travel the distance to the moon and back. A small bird called the bar-tailed godwit flies more than eleven thousand kilometres from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping, a journey that takes about a week.
paras.C: How do the birds find their way? Researchers have discovered several methods. Birds use the position of the sun during the day and the stars at night. They can also sense the magnetic field of the Earth, which works like an inner compass. In addition, many birds follow rivers, coasts and mountain ranges, and some remember the smell of places they know. Young birds often travel in the company of experienced adults who show them the route.
paras.D: Migration is dangerous. Birds meet storms, hunters and tall buildings. Lights in big cities can confuse them at night, and every year, millions die from collisions with windows. Another threat is the loss of the wetlands where they rest on the way. Without safe places to stop and feed, even the strongest birds cannot finish the journey.
paras.E: For this reason, countries around the world cooperate to protect migrating birds. They create nature reserves along the main routes, limit hunting and ask cities to switch off unnecessary lights during the migration season. Bird watchers also help by counting the birds they see and sharing the results online. Their data show where numbers are falling and where protection is needed. When a flock appears in the sky in spring, it is a sign that these efforts are working.

paras.A: In many sports, success depends not on the best individual but on the best team. A football team with eleven talented players may still lose to a team of ordinary players who understand each other. Coaches say that the difference is cooperation: players who trust their partners pass the ball at the right moment, cover for each other's mistakes and share the credit for a win.
paras.B: Building such a team takes time. In the first weeks of training, players learn each other's habits. A striker discovers that his partner always looks left before passing; a defender learns when the goalkeeper will come out. Good teams also practise communication. They use short words and simple signals on the field because there is no time for long explanations. Silent teams, coaches say, are usually losing teams.
paras.C: The leader of a team does not have to be the best player. Many successful captains are not the most skilful, but they are good at listening and at keeping everyone calm in difficult moments. A captain who shouts at his colleagues after a mistake usually makes things worse. One who says, 'Forget it, the next ball is ours', helps the team to recover quickly.
paras.D: Teamwork also teaches life skills. Young people who play in a team learn to take turns, to accept decisions they do not like and to work for a common goal. Employers often look for such experience when they hire. A job candidate who can explain how his team overcame a difficult moment in a match shows qualities that cannot easily be shown by a certificate.
paras.E: Of course, problems exist. Sometimes a player thinks only of his own fame and refuses to pass the ball. Some teams contain players who dislike each other, and the result is a lack of trust. Coaches handle these problems by speaking directly and by making the team's aims clear. As the famous saying goes, talent wins games, but teamwork wins championships.

paras.A: Glass is so common that we hardly notice it. We drink from it, look through it and see ourselves in it. Yet this material, which seems so simple, is made from some of the most ordinary things on Earth: sand, soda and limestone. When these are heated to about 1,500 degrees Celsius, they melt and, when they cool, they become hard and transparent.
paras.B: Glass is much older than most people think. Natural glass forms when lightning strikes sand or when a volcano throws out hot rock, and early humans used sharp pieces of it as knives. The first man-made glass was probably produced in the Middle East about four thousand years ago, and for many centuries, it was used for beads and small bottles. These objects were so expensive that only rich people could own them.
paras.C: A major step forward happened about two thousand years ago, when craftsmen discovered how to blow glass. A worker dipped a long tube into the melted material, blew into the other end and shaped a bubble, which could be changed into a bottle or a cup. Because the process was quick, glass became cheaper, and ordinary families began to use it. In the Islamic world, artists decorated it with gold and colours, and fine glass from Syria and Egypt was traded as far as China.
paras.D: For windows, people first used small pieces of glass connected with lead. Large clear panes were difficult to make, and until the nineteenth century, they were a sign of wealth. It is the main material for smartphone screens, and it carries information in thin threads called optical fibres, which are the basis of the internet.
paras.E: Another advantage of glass is that it can be recycled without losing quality. Old bottles can be crushed, melted and formed again as often as necessary. Each tonne of recycled glass saves a considerable amount of raw materials and energy. Many countries now have colour-coded containers in the street for this purpose, and people who use them help to turn yesterday's jar into tomorrow's window.
